metadata.title: Cassie, Caleb, and the Eye That Learned to See
metadata.subtitle: How Computers Came to See the World
metadata.tagline: Some questions are so big — and so audacious — that we taught a machine to help us look for the answers.
metadata.author: FableFlow AI
metadata.dedication_text: For Dr Fei-Fei Li — who crossed oceans, sorted shirts, and asked the audacious question that taught the world's computers to see. And for every curious child who is brave enough to ask 'how does it know?' — may you grow up to teach the machines of the future to be kind, fair, and full of wonder.

chapters.title: The Phone That Knew
chapters.text:
It was a Saturday morning, and the kind of sunshine was coming through the kitchen window that made everything look slightly magical. It turned the steam from Mum's tea into dancing ghosts. It made the buttered toast glow like little gold bricks. It even made the dust in the air look like tiny floating stars.

Cassie was sitting on the kitchen bench, swinging her legs. Her dress had bright yellow stars on it, and her brown eyes were wide and alert. She was in what she called "investigation mode" — the special mood she got into when something didn't quite add up, and she was determined to find out why. Under the table, three-year-old Caleb was busy building a wobbly skyscraper out of empty cereal boxes. Every few seconds a box would tumble, and Caleb would let out a giggle that sounded like a bubbling brook.

Mum was leaning against the counter, scrolling through photos on her phone. She was smiling at the screen as if she were chatting with old friends.

"Look at this one," Mum said, tilting the screen toward Cassie. "You and Caleb at the beach last summer. Look at those sandy toes!"

Cassie leaned in. She loved that photo. She could almost smell the salt in the air and feel the warm sand crunching under her feet.

"And this one," Mum said with a quick swipe of her thumb. "You at Grandma's birthday party, wearing that giant purple hat. Oh — and here's all of us at Diwali, look how the diyas glow."

Cassie watched the photos blur past, hundreds of them, each one neatly tucked inside little folders. She frowned. She was impressed. But she was also thinking.

"Mum," she said, "how did you find those so fast? You didn't even have to look through all the photos from the whole year."

"The phone sorts them for me," Mum explained. She tapped a little circle on the screen. "See? It has a folder for 'Caleb'. It has a folder for 'Cassie'. It even has a folder for 'Beach' and 'Dogs' and 'Sunsets'."

Cassie blinked. She looked at the phone. Then she looked at Caleb, who had just decided that a cereal box made an excellent helmet. He was currently marching around the kitchen, humming a song only he knew.

"But Mum," Cassie said slowly, "how does it know that's Caleb? The phone doesn't have eyes. It's just a piece of glass and metal. It can't see his curly hair or his gap-toothed smile. So how does it actually *know*?"

Mum opened her mouth to answer. Then she closed it. She looked at the phone, then back at Cassie's curious face. Then she did something Cassie loved more than almost anything else.

"You know what, sweetheart," Mum said honestly, "I'm not entirely sure."

Cassie sat very still. In Cassie's experience, this was the most exciting thing a grown-up could ever say. When a grown-up knew the answer, the story ended. But when a grown-up *didn't* know — that meant there was a mystery to chase, a corner of the world that hadn't been mapped yet. And Cassie loved unmapped corners more than chocolate.

"Maybe it's magic," Caleb shouted from under the table, his cereal-box helmet slipping over his eyes.

"It's not magic, Caleb," Cassie whispered, though she felt a little spark of magic in her chest. "It's a *secret*. And I want to find out what it is."

Mum smiled and held the phone closer. "Well, if we want to find a secret, we might need a map. Or a museum." She tapped the screen again and showed Cassie a bright, colourful advertisement.

The letters were bold and bouncy. They read: **HOW COMPUTERS SEE — A FAMILY EXHIBITION at the Powerhouse Museum.**

"I think," said Mum, "we might have somewhere to go today."

"GO!" Caleb yelled, throwing his arms up so that the cereal-box helmet flew off completely. "GO TO THE MUSEUM!"

Cassie was already half-off the bench. But before she ran for her shoes, she took Mum's phone, held it close to her nose, and stared at the picture of Caleb until something funny happened. The picture started to break apart.

"Mum! Look!" she cried. "If I look really close, the picture isn't a picture at all. It's just thousands of tiny, tiny squares of colour!"

Mum leaned in. "That's right, my love. Those tiny squares are called **pixels**. A pixel is the smallest little dot of colour a screen can show. We'll learn much more about them today — and about how a pile of dots can become a face."

Cassie stared at the squares. She stared until her eyes went a bit blurry. The face she knew so well — Caleb's soft brown cheeks, his bouncing curls, his tiny chipped front tooth — had dissolved into a mosaic of coloured boxes. And yet, when she pulled the phone away again, Caleb popped back into view, as if he had been there all along.

"So the pixels are the pieces," Cassie whispered. "But how does the phone know which pieces make a face? And how does it know which face is *Caleb's*?"

Mum squeezed her shoulder. "That, Cassie, is exactly what we are going to find out."

Cassie didn't just walk to the door. She zoomed. She found her shoes in record time. She put them on the wrong feet, fixed them, and put them on again. Her notebook went into her backpack. Her favourite pencil went in beside it. Investigation mode was on full power. She was going to the Powerhouse Museum, and she wasn't coming home until she had cracked the secret of the pixels.
chapters.poem:
A picture on a screen
Looks finished, looks complete —
Until you zoom in close,
And the colours all repeat.

A grid of tiny squares,
A mosaic, neat and bright,
Each one a little pixel,
A little drop of light.

The phone sees only pieces,
A pattern, line by line —
But how does it know Caleb?
That's the puzzle, yours and mine.

questions: What are the tiny squares of colour called that make up a picture on a screen?
Why did Cassie find it exciting when Mum said 'I'm not entirely sure'? What does that tell you about how scientists feel about questions they can't yet answer?
Have you ever looked very, very closely at something and noticed it was made of smaller pieces? What did you see?

chapters.title: Pixels on the Train
chapters.text:
The train rattled towards the city, humming a low, steady song. Sunlight flickered through the windows like a slideshow, lighting up Cassie's honey-brown skin in stripes. Mum's phone rested in her lap, glowing like a magic mirror. Opposite her, Caleb was busy. He was kicking his legs and counting telephone poles as they whizzed past.

"One... two... five... ten!" Caleb shouted.

Cassie smiled. Caleb's counting was more like guessing, but he did it with such passion that it felt like he was winning a race. Some passengers nearby smiled too.

Cassie looked back at the screen. She wanted to see, properly this time, how the phone hid all those tiny squares inside a single face. She remembered the way Mum's fingers moved, so she pinched the screen and pulled her fingers apart. The photo grew bigger. Then bigger. Then bigger.

And then, something funny happened.

Caleb's face — the soft brown cheeks, the curly black hair, the gap-toothed grin — began to break apart.

First, the edges became fuzzy, like a painting left out in the rain. Then the fuzziness turned into squares. Finally, the image dissolved into thousands of tiny, tiny coloured squares, lined up neatly like a mosaic floor or a piece of graph paper.

"Caleb," Cassie whispered. "Look."

Caleb scrambled across the seat, his light-up sneakers flashing red and blue. He pressed his nose so hard against the screen that it flattened.

"That's me?" he asked, his voice muffled.

"That's you," said Cassie. "But really, really close up."

Mum leaned in, her kind eyes twinkling. "You've found the secret ingredients of the picture, Cassie."

"Ingredients?" Cassie asked. "Like flour and sugar?"

"In a way," Mum replied. "These little squares are pixels — remember? But here's the part nobody tells you. To a computer, a pixel isn't actually a colour at all. It's a *number*."

Cassie blinked. "A number?"

"Yes," Mum said. "Imagine that every shade of colour has a secret code. Bright red might be 'two-fifty-five, zero, zero'. Sky blue might be 'one-twenty, two-hundred, two-fifty'. The computer doesn't see 'red' or 'blue' the way your eyes do. It just reads a giant grid of numbers — millions of them — and the numbers are the picture."

Cassie looked at the screen. She tried to imagine the photo of Caleb as a grid of numbers instead of colours. The brown of his cheek would be some number. The dark of his hair, another. The little white spark on his tooth, another. It was like a colouring book where every square already had its instructions written inside.

"So the phone doesn't see a face?" Cassie asked. "It just sees... numbers?"

"Exactly," Mum said. "And those numbers come with a label — that's the next clue. A label is a name we attach to a pattern of numbers so the computer knows what they mean. We tell the computer, 'When you see a pattern of numbers that looks roughly like this, the label is *Caleb*.' Then, when it sees a new picture, it checks: do these new numbers look like the Caleb pattern? If they do, the label sticks."

Caleb looked at his arm. He poked it. He sniffed it. He looked back at the screen, very suspicious.

"I not numbers," he said firmly.

"Don't worry," Cassie giggled, hugging him. "You're not numbers in real life. You're made of... well, you. Bones and squishy bits and lots of laughing."

Caleb seemed satisfied with that. He went back to counting telephone poles.

"Eleven! Twelve! Million!" he shouted.

But Cassie stayed quiet. She kept zooming. In and out. In and out. She watched the world shift from Caleb-the-boy to Caleb-the-pattern, and back again. She got out her notebook and tried to draw what she was seeing — a tidy grid of squares, each one a different shade. It was harder than it looked.

She wondered about the phone's brain. If the phone only saw a sea of numbers, how did it know where the nose ended and the cheek began? How did it know that a smudge of dark wasn't a shadow, or a piece of chocolate, or a piece of hair?

It must be very, very confused most of the time, she thought. It was like trying to read a story when somebody had cut every letter into tiny pieces of confetti and tossed them into the air.

Cassie looked out the window. A ladybug had landed on the glass. She leaned in close — very, very close — until the ladybug's shiny red shell filled her whole view. And then, for just a second, she imagined she could see it too: the bug's smooth shell breaking into tiny, glowing pixels, each one a little number waiting to be added up.

Even ladybugs, she thought, are made of dots, if you look at them the right way.

"I'm going to figure it out," she whispered to the ladybug. "I'm going to find out how the dots — and the numbers — become a *person*."

The ladybug, who had no idea it was being whispered to, opened its wings and flew away.
chapters.poem:
A picture is a puzzle
Of squares all in a row,
And every square's a number
The computer comes to know.

A code for every colour,
A code for every shade,
That's how a smile, or a sky,
Or a ladybug is made.

But numbers can't see faces —
They only count and sum.
So someone has to teach them
What the patterns have become.

chapters.title: Teaching the Robot
chapters.text:
The Powerhouse Museum smelled, as it always did, of polished wood and faintly of glue. Cassie loved it instantly. It felt like a place where things were being put together, or taken apart, or imagined for the first time.

A sign with a friendly cartoon robot pointed them down a corridor lit in soft blues and teals: *HOW COMPUTERS SEE — THIS WAY!*

The first thing they came to was a touchscreen table called The Sorting Game. On the screen was the cartoon robot, who looked rather like a friendly toaster with eyes. Around him were dozens of pictures, floating like digital confetti. Three empty piles at the bottom of the screen were labelled: **CAT**, **DOG**, and **NOT A CAT OR A DOG**.

"Easy," said Cassie.

She began to drag the pictures with her finger. A tabby with stripes — CAT. A golden retriever with a floppy tongue — DOG. A bright yellow banana — NOT.

Cassie felt like a pro. But as she kept sliding pictures, the robot started to look confused. The pictures weren't so simple anymore.

A tiger appeared. Cassie paused. A tiger had whiskers. It had pointy ears. It had a long tail. It looked like a cat — a very big, very stripy cat. Cassie hesitated, then dropped it into the CAT pile.

The friendly toaster blinked. "Hmm," it said in a metallic chirp. "Are you sure?"

Then came a fox. It had a bushy tail and a pointed nose. It looked like a dog. Or maybe a cat? Cassie frowned. She decided to play it safe and dropped it into the NOT pile.

Then came a sphynx cat — bald, wrinkly, and not fluffy at all. Cassie squinted. It didn't look like any cat she had ever met. But it had pointy ears and giant yellow eyes, so she put it in CAT.

Then came the trickiest one of all. It was a picture of a slipper. But it wasn't a normal slipper; it was white, weirdly fluffy, and had two shiny black button eyes. It looked exactly like a sleeping kitten.

Caleb leaned over, his chubby cheek pressing against Cassie's shoulder. He pointed a small finger at the screen and said firmly, "Cat."

Cassie giggled and dragged the slipper into the CAT pile.

When they had sorted twenty pictures, the toaster gave them a score. *Sixteen out of twenty.*

"Sixteen!" Cassie frowned. "I thought I *knew* what a cat was."

Mum knelt down beside her. "You do know what a cat is, Cassie. But there is a big difference between *knowing* something and *teaching* it. Knowing happens quietly in your head. Teaching means turning that quiet thing into words and rules and examples, so somebody else can learn it too. And teaching is much harder."

"But I told him!" Cassie pointed at the toaster. "I put the cats in the cat pile!"

"You gave him **examples**," Mum explained. "An example is one of many things you look at to learn a pattern. When you see a cat, your brain doesn't just remember one picture. It remembers every cat you've ever seen — the fluffy ones, the skinny ones, the ones that purr and the ones that hiss, the ones in books and the ones that wind around your ankles. Your brain builds a kind of secret 'cat-feeling' from all of them. But a computer doesn't have a brain like yours. It only has numbers and patterns."

"So he's not actually seeing the cat?" Cassie asked. "He's just counting dots?"

"He's looking for the pattern," Mum said. "And sometimes — like with the fluffy slipper — the pattern tricks him. The slipper had two black dots that looked like eyes. It had soft, pale fluff. To you and me, it's obviously a slipper. To the robot, those numbers added up to *cat*."

Cassie turned to Caleb. She wanted to see if her brother's brain worked the same way as the toaster's brain.

"Caleb," she said seriously. "What's a cat?"

Caleb thought about it. He scrunched up his nose. "Meow," he said.

"And what about a tiger?"

"Big meow."

"And a fluffy slipper with eyes?"

Caleb looked at the screen, then at his own toes, then back at the screen. He leaned in and whispered, very firmly, "Silly."

Cassie beamed. "See?" she told the toaster. "He figured it out in three tries. He knows what's a cat and what's just *silly*. How many tries did *you* need?"

The screen below the toaster lit up with a giant number. It read: *I LEARNED THIS BY LOOKING AT 1,500,000 PICTURES.*

Cassie stared. She tried to imagine a million of anything. A million pebbles? A million stars? A million bowls of porridge?

"One million five hundred thousand," she whispered.

She did a quick sum in her head, the way Mum had taught her. If she looked at one picture every single second, with no stopping for food or sleep, she would need more than two whole weeks to look at a million pictures. And the robot had looked at one and a half million. *Just to learn what a cat was.*

"That's a lot of cats," Cassie said. "I think I'd get bored of looking at that many cats."

"And here's the curious thing," Mum said. "Even after a million and a half pictures, the robot still got tricked by a slipper. Caleb only needed to hear 'meow' a few times, and he can spot a cat across the room. Your brain is much, much better at this than the robot's. The robot has to look at a mountain of pictures to do what a toddler can do over breakfast."

Cassie looked at Caleb, who was currently testing whether his light-up sneakers worked if he jumped very high. They did. They flashed wildly with every landing.

"That's why the robot needs our help," Mum said, guiding them gently toward the next exhibit. "He has the numbers. But he doesn't have the *silly*. That part still belongs to us."
chapters.poem:
A million pictures, a million tries,
To learn what's fluff and what's got eyes.
The robot studies, slow and steady —
A toddler knows before he's ready.

Numbers, patterns, codes, and dots —
The robot counts, the robot plots.
But silly slippers fool him still,
A child's brain works with quicker skill.

So teaching means more than telling true,
It means the many, not the few.

questions: What is the difference between *knowing* something and *teaching* it? Can you think of a time you tried to teach somebody something you knew well, and it was harder than you thought?
Why did the friendly toaster-robot need to look at one and a half million pictures, when Caleb only needed to hear 'meow' a few times?
If you were teaching a robot to recognise your favourite toy, what kinds of *different* pictures of it would you show? Try to think of at least five.

chapters.title: A Wall of Everything
chapters.text:
They turned a corner and stopped walking.

In front of them, from floor to ceiling, was a wall made entirely of photographs. Tiny ones. Hundreds and hundreds — no, thousands — all in neat little squares. Each photo had a label beneath it in cheerful, clear letters.

APPLE. SUNSET. DINGO. DOSA. DAFFODIL. KITE. KOOKABURRA. KETTLE.

Cassie felt very small. She felt like a tiny ant standing at the foot of a mountain made of memories. The wall shimmered under the museum lights, a mosaic of everything in the world. There were photos of fluffy clouds, rusty bicycles, sliced mangoes, sleepy kittens, paper aeroplanes, and one rather grumpy-looking iguana.

"Mum," Cassie breathed. "Mum, *look*. It's everything!"

Then her eyes landed on a square near her shoulder and her whole face lit up.

"DOSA!" she cried. "Mum, it knows about dosa! It has a *picture of a dosa*!"

It was, in fact, a beautiful golden dosa, curled into a perfect crisp roll on a banana leaf, with a tiny bowl of coconut chutney beside it. Cassie could almost smell it.

"It does," Mum smiled. "Of course it does. Dosas are part of the world too."

Caleb waddled forward. His light-up sneakers blinked red and blue as he leaned in close. He pointed a chubby finger at a bright yellow square in the bottom corner.

"Nana!" he said proudly.

It was, in fact, a picture of a banana.

"Exactly!" Cassie cried. She beamed at her brother. She felt a little spark of pride in her chest. "See, Caleb? That's a banana because it's yellow and curved. You're getting really good at this!"

Mum stepped closer to the wall and pointed to a gold plaque bolted to the side.

"This wall is inspired by a real collection of pictures called **ImageNet**," Mum read aloud. "ImageNet contains over fourteen million labelled photographs — gathered, named, and organised by people all around the world. It was built by a scientist called Dr Fei-Fei Li, who wanted to give computers something they had never had before: enough examples to learn from."

"Fee-Fee Lee," Cassie repeated. The name felt bouncy in her mouth, like trying on a new pair of shoes.

"Fei-Fei," Mum corrected gently.

Cassie tried again. "Fei-Fei. Fei-Fei Li." This time it stayed put.

"And it took thousands and thousands of people to help her," Mum added. "People all over the world looked at pictures and typed in the right words underneath. Imagine all those people, in all those countries, sitting at their kitchen tables and saying, 'This is a dosa. This is a kookaburra. This is a kettle.'"

Cassie tried to picture it. A man in Mumbai labelling rickshaws. A grandmother in Mexico labelling cactuses. A teenager in Tokyo labelling cherry blossoms. A young woman in Sydney, perhaps, labelling a kookaburra she saw outside her window. Millions of pictures named by tens of thousands of helpers. The wall in front of her wasn't really a wall, she realised. It was a kind of *gift* — a gift from many, many people to a machine that couldn't see.

"But why did she need so many?" Cassie asked. "In the game before, the robot only needed a few cats. Why fourteen million?"

Mum knelt down so she was eye-level with Cassie. "Think about how you learned what a dog is, Cassie. Did you only see one golden retriever and decide that *all* dogs are golden and fluffy?"

Cassie giggled. "No. I saw the neighbour's tiny poodle. And the big, grumpy bulldog at the park. And the skinny greyhound on TV. And Auntie's hairy little terrier."

"Exactly," said Mum. "To really understand a 'dog', you have to see thousands of different dogs. You have to see dogs in the rain and dogs on couches. Dogs from the side, dogs from the top, dogs hiding behind a curtain with only their tail showing. Dr Fei-Fei Li realised that computers were struggling not because they were stupid, but because they didn't have a big enough **dataset**."

"A data-set?" Cassie asked.

"Yes," Mum explained. "A dataset is just a fancy word for a great big pile of examples gathered together for learning. Imagine if you tried to learn what a 'chair' was, but I only ever showed you one wooden stool. You might think all chairs have to be wooden and have no back! But if I gave you a dataset of ten thousand chairs — plastic ones, velvet ones, office chairs that spin, deckchairs, beanbags, even a throne — your brain would start to see the pattern. You'd learn that a chair is anything you can sit on. Dr Fei-Fei Li built a *giant* dataset, on purpose, so the computer could see every kind of dog and chair and banana in the world. Not just the easy ones."

Cassie looked up at the wall again. She tried to imagine fourteen million pictures. She couldn't, quite — her brain couldn't hold a number that big. But she could imagine the *work*. She imagined someone, a young woman with kind eyes and a very determined look, patiently labelling them. And next to her, ten more people. And next to them, hundreds more. And spreading out from there, like ripples on a pond, thousands of people in dozens of countries, all helping.

*This is a cat. This is a car. This is a cupcake. This is a dosa.*

One after another, after another, after another. It sounded like the hardest homework assignment in history. But it also sounded like a *gift*. It was as though Dr Fei-Fei Li and her helpers had been quietly building a library of the whole world — not for people to read, but for a machine to study.

Caleb was still staring at the banana. He pointed to a picture of a lemon next to it.

"Nana?" he asked, unsure.

Cassie leaned in. "Not quite, Caleb. Look at the shape. This one is rounder and smaller. This is a lemon. See? Same yellow, different shape."

Caleb nodded solemnly. "Lemon."

Cassie smiled. She was helping Caleb build his own little dataset, one fruit at a time.

"I like her," Cassie whispered, thinking of the scientist somewhere on the other side of the world. "I really would like to meet her."
chapters.poem:
A million eyes have done this work,
From Sydney, Tokyo, Mumbai —
They wrote the names beneath the dots
So robot eyes could learn to spy.

A dosa. Daffodil. A drum.
A dingo. Doorknob. Daisy chain.
Each tiny picture, tagged and tucked,
A gift, a clue, a labelled grain.

The more we show, the more they know —
That's how a robot's eyes begin to grow.

The wall glows like a digital mountain under museum lights. illustrations.description: A conceptual, dreamlike illustration in soft-focus watercolour. In the background, a ghostly young woman with kind eyes, dark hair, and a quietly determined expression — a younger Dr Fei-Fei Li — is shown patiently labelling photos at a desk piled with papers, surrounded by floating labels: DOG, CHAIR, APPLE, DOSA, KITE, SUNSET. Around her, in fainter outline, dozens of other helpers from around the world also sit at their kitchen tables, also labelling — figures of all ages and skin tones, each with their own small lamp of light. Mood: connection across time and across the world, the quiet heroism of patient work.

chapters.title: The Machine That Said 'Moon'
chapters.text:
The See-and-Say Booth was Caleb's favourite thing in the museum, possibly forever.

It looked like a little wooden hut with a camera perched on top like a curious bird. On the front was a big silver speaker that looked like a giant ear. The rules were simple: you stepped inside the booth, held an object up to the camera, and the speaker told you, in a cheerful robotic voice, what it thought you were holding.

Caleb tried to climb in first, but his light-up sneakers were too excited and he kept bouncing on the spot.

"My turn! My turn!" he cheered.

"Wait, Caleb," Cassie said, holding up her sketchbook. "I want to see if it knows my art."

Cassie stepped into the booth. It smelled faintly of old libraries and electricity. She took a deep breath and held up her drawing of a dog. It was a golden retriever with a very long tongue and floppy ears.

The camera clicked. The machine hummed.

"Dog!" the speaker announced.

Cassie beamed. Her dimples popped. "It works! It really *sees*!"

She felt a surge of confidence. She reached for the next page and held up her drawing of a cat. It was a fluffy ginger cat, curled up in a ball, looking very sleepy.

The camera clicked. The machine hummed.

"Rabbit!" the speaker shouted.

Cassie blinked. She looked at the drawing. She looked at the camera. She held the cat up again, tilting it to the left.

"Rabbit!" the machine insisted, in exactly the same cheerful voice.

"It's not a rabbit," Cassie protested. "It has whiskers! And a long tail! Rabbits have *short* tails!"

But the machine didn't care about whiskers. It just liked the word 'rabbit'.

Cassie turned the page and held up the paratha she had drawn that morning at breakfast — a flat, round, slightly squiggly circle with little brown spots.

"Cookie!" the speaker said brightly.

Cassie laughed. "It's a *paratha*! Have you never seen a paratha?"

The machine, of course, had not.

Then Cassie decided to try something audacious. *Audacious* means being brave and a little bit cheeky, in the best possible way. She flipped to the back of her book and held up her drawing of Dad.

It was a stick figure. Dad had a very round head, no hair, and a very small triangle for a body. He looked like a little person wearing a giant party hat.

The machine paused. It hummed for a long time, as if it were thinking very hard.

"Moon!" the speaker said confidently.

Cassie howled. She laughed so hard she had to sit down on the floor of the booth. Caleb started laughing because Cassie was laughing. Mum laughed because nobody could possibly resist the idea of Dad being a glowing white moon up in the sky.

When the giggles finally stopped, Cassie sat very still. She looked at the camera. She looked at her drawings. She felt a little puzzle forming in her mind, like pieces of a jigsaw slowly fitting together.

"Mum," Cassie said, her voice thoughtful. "*How does it know?*"

Mum leaned against the wooden frame of the booth. "That is the big question, isn't it? Why was it right about the dog, but wrong about the cat, and the paratha, and Dad?"

"I think," Cassie said slowly, "somebody showed it lots and lots of dogs. Real dogs. Brown dogs, spotted dogs, tiny dogs, fluffy dogs."

"And?" Mum asked.

"And maybe not very many cats," Cassie guessed. "Or maybe the cats it saw didn't look like my sleepy ginger one. Maybe it only saw cats standing up, not curled in balls."

"And the paratha?"

"Probably it had never seen a paratha at all," Cassie said. "But it had seen lots of cookies. So when it saw something round and brown and flat, it guessed 'cookie' because that was the closest word it had."

Mum nodded. "You've figured it out. This machine uses something called a **training set**. Imagine a giant digital scrapbook filled with millions of pictures. The pictures inside the scrapbook are the only things the machine has ever seen. If the scrapbook has ten thousand pictures of dogs but only ten cats, the machine becomes an expert on dogs and a beginner with cats. And if it has no parathas at all — not one — it has to guess. So it picks the closest thing it knows."

"So it's like when Caleb tried to learn his colours?" Cassie asked.

"Exactly," Mum said. "Caleb knows 'red' really well because lots of things in his toy box are red. But he calls eggplant 'blue' because nobody's shown him 'purple' enough times yet. The machine isn't actually *thinking* the way you and I think — it's just looking for the closest pattern in its scrapbook."

Cassie looked at the drawing of Dad. "So it didn't see a person. It just saw a round, white shape."

"Right," said Mum. "And in its scrapbook, the most common round, white shape is the moon. It didn't see Dad. It saw a pattern that reminded it of the sky."

Cassie smiled. The machine wasn't magic, and it wasn't really 'smart' the way a person is smart. It was just a very fast student that only knew what its teachers had shown it — and when something brand new came along, it tried its best to fit the new thing into an old idea.

She tucked her sketchbook away and thought about how easy it would be to teach a machine the wrong things. If nobody ever showed it parathas, it would just keep calling them cookies forever. If nobody ever showed it a dad, it would keep calling round-headed people the moon. The machine couldn't *ask*. It could only guess from what it had.

Caleb, seeing that the laughing was over, pushed his way into the booth. He held up his stuffed elephant, which was missing one ear and smelled faintly of peanut butter.

"Elephant!" the speaker shouted.

Caleb nodded gravely, as if this had been the correct answer all along.
chapters.poem:
A circle for a head,
A triangle for a chest —
The machine guessed "Moon",
And put our Dad to the test.

A paratha became a cookie,
A cat became a hare —
The machine knows only what it's seen,
And not what isn't there.

So if we want a smarter eye,
A fairer one, a true —
We must show it parathas,
And dads, and ginger cats too.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Asked Audacious Questions
chapters.text:
The Story Auditorium was a small, dark room that smelled faintly of old popcorn and velvet. It had rows of plush red seats and a giant screen at the front. Cassie chose a seat right in the middle, the perfect spot for seeing everything. Caleb chose the chair next to her, then immediately swapped to the chair next to that one, then swapped back again, his light-up sneakers flashing red and blue in the dim light.

"Shhh," Cassie whispered, though Caleb wasn't making any noise — he was just vibrating with excitement.

The lights dimmed until the room was as dark as the inside of a wardrobe. Then the screen flickered to life.

A woman appeared. She had warm brown eyes, dark hair pulled neatly back, and a smile that reached her cheeks. She was sitting in front of a bookshelf filled with heavy volumes. Beneath her, in soft white letters, it read: **DR FEI-FEI LI**.

"Hello, curious friends," said Dr Li. Her voice was warm and a little musical, like a song you almost remember. "My name is Fei-Fei."

Cassie sat very still. She leaned forward, her chin resting in her palms.

"I want to tell you a story," Dr Li said. "It begins a long way from here, in a city in China called Chengdu, where I was a curious child just like you. I loved reading. I asked too many questions. My favourite question was 'why?' and my second favourite was 'how?', and I never got tired of asking them.

"When I was about fifteen years old, my family did a very big thing. We packed up our whole life and moved across the ocean to a small town in America called Parsippany, in the state of New Jersey. I didn't speak any English. Not one word."

Cassie looked at Mum. She tried to imagine being fifteen and having to start over in a country where every sign, every menu, every joke was in a language she didn't understand.

"It was hard," Dr Li said. "I missed home. The food was different. The school was different. The other children were kind but they couldn't understand me, and I couldn't understand them. So I did what curious children do. I watched. I listened. I read every label I could find. I learned new English words from cereal boxes and street signs and the back of milk cartons.

"My family worked very hard. My parents and I ran a little shop that cleaned other people's clothes. I helped after school and on weekends. I answered the telephone. I sorted the shirts. I learned new English words by reading the labels on the tags. And in between customers, I did my homework on the counter."

Cassie imagined the shop. She imagined rows and rows of crisp white shirts, all hanging in a long line, each with a tiny white tag like a little name-card. She imagined Fei-Fei reading those tags, picking up an English word here and an English word there, the way you might pick up shells on a beach.

"I had a maths teacher in high school called Mr Sabella," Dr Li went on. "He saw that I was curious, and he believed in me when many other people couldn't see past my accent. He gave me books to read. He helped my family. Sometimes one kind grown-up is all the difference in the world. I hope every one of you has, or finds, your own Mr Sabella one day."

Cassie's heart felt warm.

"And the whole time," Dr Li said, "I kept asking questions. Big ones. Small ones. Audacious ones."

Cassie blinked. "Mum?" she whispered. "What does *audacious* mean?"

Mum leaned in close. "Audacious is a fancy word for being very, very brave with your ideas," she whispered back. "It's when you ask a question that other people might think is too wild, or too impossible, or too big."

Cassie liked that. She felt audacious every time she asked why the sky was blue or where the wind went when it stopped blowing.

"One day," Dr Li continued, "when I was at university, I started asking a strange question. I was watching babies. I had noticed something extraordinary. When a baby is born, she sees thousands and thousands of things, every day, for years. Faces. Spoons. Dogs. Daffodils. The sky. The patterns on the curtains. The shape of her own hand. Slowly, slowly, she learns what each one is. Nobody sits her down and gives her a lesson. She just *looks*, and the world teaches her."

Caleb pointed at his own nose. "I see nose!" he whispered loudly.

"And I thought," Dr Li said, "what if a computer needed the same? What if computers had been getting stuck not because they were broken, but because nobody had ever given them enough pictures to look at? What if they were like babies who had been kept in a quiet, empty room?"

Cassie nodded so hard her wavy black hair bounced. She remembered the robot from the Sorting Game. She remembered the cookie and the moon. The robot wasn't dumb. It was hungry — hungry for more pictures, more examples, more of the world.

"So my friends and I made a great big collection of pictures," Dr Li said. "We called it **ImageNet**. Fourteen million pictures, organised into more than twenty thousand kinds of thing. Apples and zebras, mangoes and bicycles, sneezes and sunsets. Every single picture had a name written carefully beside it. It took us years. We had help from tens of thousands of people, all over the world. And when we finally showed our collection to the machines, something magical happened. The machines began to learn to see. Not all at once. Slowly, slowly. But every year they got better. And the computers we have today — the ones in your phones and tablets and cars — can do what they do because somewhere, a long time ago, a girl who had been a dry-cleaner's daughter wondered if computers might learn the way babies do."

Cassie thought about the Million Pictures Wall in the next room. She thought about the dosa, and the kookaburra, and the kettle. She thought about all the hands and voices and patient hours that had gone into a wall she had walked past in less than a minute. It wasn't magic, she realised. It was just an enormous amount of *looking*, done together.

"Now I work at a place called Stanford University," Dr Li said. "I teach. I do research. And I help run two groups very close to my heart. One is called the **Human-Centered AI Institute**. We try to make sure that the machines being built today are kind, and fair, and useful for *people* — not just clever for their own sake. The other is called **AI4ALL**. We invite all kinds of children — girls, children from countries that don't usually get invited, children whose families don't have much money — to come and learn about AI. Because the future of these machines belongs to all of us. Not just a few.

"If there is one thing I would love for you to take home today," Dr Li said, her eyes twinkling on the screen, "it is this. The best discoveries start with a question that feels a little bit too big. The kind of question that makes grown-ups laugh nervously, or scratch their heads, or say, 'Hmm, I'm not entirely sure.' Don't be afraid of those questions. They are not silly. They are *audacious*. Ask them anyway. Ask them again. And when you grow up, please — keep asking."

The screen went dark. The house lights came up slowly, turning the red velvet seats bright again.

For a long moment, Cassie didn't move. She felt as if a secret door had opened inside her mind. The phone in Mum's pocket and the robot in the Sorting Game and the machine in the See-and-Say Booth weren't born smart. They were *taught*. They were students. And Dr Fei-Fei Li had been one of their first teachers — a girl, once, who didn't speak the language, who worked at a counter sorting shirts, who kept asking the question nobody else was asking.

"Mum," Cassie said quietly. "I think she just answered my question."

Mum put a warm arm around her shoulders and kissed the top of her head. "Which question, sweetheart?"

Cassie smiled, her dimples showing in the dim auditorium light.

"All of them."
chapters.poem:
She crossed a sea, she sorted shirts,
She read the labels one by one,
She asked the question no one asked
Beneath the New Jersey sun.

What if the robot is a baby?
What if it just needs to see?
What if a wall of named-up pictures
Is the gift that sets it free?

A girl who didn't speak the language
Taught a machine to look —
And every picture on her wall
Is a page in the world's great book.

So if your question feels too big,
Too wild, too odd to share —
Be like Fei-Fei. Ask it anyway.
Audacious is brave, and fair.

chapters.title: The Aha
chapters.text:
Outside the auditorium, the museum corridor was suddenly a river of people. There were shouting children, clicking cameras, and the sweet, cold smell of vanilla ice cream. Caleb was trailing behind, his light-up sneakers flashing red-blue-red with every wobbling step.

Cassie barely noticed the noise. Her mind was humming. It felt like a puzzle that had finally clicked into place — that wonderful, fizzing feeling when a thousand tiny pieces suddenly make one big, clear picture.

She stopped walking. She looked at the phone in Mum's hand. Then she looked at Caleb. Then she looked back at the auditorium door, where Dr Fei-Fei Li's voice was still echoing in her head.

"Mum," Cassie said, her voice small but sure. "I think I get it."

Mum stopped and turned, her expression open and encouraging. "Tell me everything."

Cassie took a deep breath. She held up one finger.

"The phone knew Caleb," she said, "because it saw a thousand little pieces of him. It saw his curly hair. It saw his gap-toothed smile. It saw his chubby cheeks. Someone showed the phone lots and lots of pictures of Caleb and said, 'This is Caleb. This is also Caleb. This is Caleb, too.' So now when it sees a new photo with that pattern, it knows. The phone isn't really 'seeing' Caleb. It's seeing a pattern of numbers that matches the Caleb pattern in its memory."

"Exactly," said Mum.

Cassie held up a second finger.

"And the machine at the booth called Dad a moon," she continued, a giggle bubbling up, "because nobody showed it Dad. Not even once. It looked at the round head with no hair and thought, *Hmm, I've never seen a Dad, but I have seen a million moons, and they are both round and pale.* So it picked moon. It wasn't being silly. It was just picking the closest thing it knew."

Mum smiled, her eyes crinkling.

"And the paratha was a cookie," Cassie added, "for exactly the same reason. The machine had probably never even *met* a paratha."

"You've figured out the secret," Mum said. "Computers don't 'know' things the way you and I know things. They find patterns. They look for shapes and colours and numbers that repeat. When something matches a pattern they've seen before, they put a label on it. When something doesn't match, they pick the closest label and hope for the best."

"Like how I taught Caleb what a banana is!" Cassie exclaimed. She pointed to Caleb, who was currently trying to balance a napkin on his head with mixed success. "I pointed at the yellow fruit and said 'banana'. Then I pointed at a picture of a banana and said 'banana'. I was giving him a label for the shape. I was being his Fei-Fei!"

"That's exactly how it works," Mum said. "Scientists call that 'labelled data'. It's like a giant library of flashcards. On one side is the picture — the pixels, the numbers — and on the other side is the name. The computer looks at the flashcards over and over until it can guess the name without even seeing the back. And the bigger the library, and the more *different* kinds of pictures it has, the better the computer becomes."

Cassie stood very still. She thought about the Million Pictures Wall. She thought about the rows of shirts in Fei-Fei's dry-cleaning shop. She thought about the tens of thousands of people in dozens of countries who had sat at their kitchen tables and typed the words *dog, cat, tree, car, cloud, dosa, kookaburra* under millions of photos.

"But Mum," Cassie asked, her brow furrowing. "Who *decides* what to show the computer? Who picks the pictures that go on the flashcards? Who chooses the labels?"

Mum knelt down. She didn't answer right away. She waited until they were eye to eye, her voice becoming soft and serious.

"That," Mum said, "is the most important question you have asked all day."

Cassie waited, her heart beating a little faster.

"People decide," Mum explained gently. "People like Dr Fei-Fei. Imagine if the person picking the pictures only chose photos of golden retrievers. If the computer only ever saw golden, fluffy dogs, what would it think when it met a little black poodle?"

"It would think the poodle wasn't a dog!" Cassie gasped.

"Right," said Mum. "It would be wrong, because the person teaching it hadn't been *thorough*. It only knew a small slice of the dog world. Now imagine bigger things. Imagine if the computer was only ever shown faces from one country, and never met faces from anywhere else. What would happen then?"

Cassie's eyes went wide. "It would only know one kind of face. It might not even *see* the others."

"Exactly," Mum said. "That's why we need people who care about getting it right. People who want the computer to see *everyone* and *everything* — not just the people they know, or the foods they eat, or the places they've been. We need people who are fair, and kind, and very, very careful. We need people who notice what's missing. Did the computer ever meet a paratha? Did it ever meet a dosa? Did it ever meet a curly-haired toddler who likes to wear cereal boxes on his head?"

Cassie giggled.

"And if the people aren't kind?" Cassie asked, her voice quieter now. "Or if they don't notice what's missing?"

"Then the machine learns the wrong things," Mum said simply. "It might learn to be unfair. It might learn to ignore people. It might learn that only *some* faces count as faces. Which is why the world needs more than just smart computers. It needs smart, curious, kind people to guide them. People who ask 'Why?' and 'Is this fair?' and 'Whose dosa is missing?' People like Fei-Fei. And people like you."

Cassie looked down at her shoes. She looked at Caleb, who had finally got most of his ice cream into his mouth, though some of it had ended up on his ear. She looked back at the gleaming museum walls, filled with the quiet ghosts of a million labelled pictures.

She didn't feel like a little girl in a big museum anymore. She felt like a detective. She felt like a teacher. She felt, just a little bit, like a scientist.

She thought, very seriously, that when she grew up, she would like to be one of the people holding the flashcards — one of the people making sure that the computers of the world learned to see *all* of it. Every face. Every food. Every kind of dog. Every curly-haired brother.
chapters.poem:
A pattern, a label, a flashcard, a name,
A library built so the robot can play the game.
But who builds the library? Who picks the books?
Who chooses the faces the robot then looks?

The teacher must be careful, the teacher must be fair,
The teacher must notice the things that aren't there.
A missing paratha, a missing kind face —
A library is only as wide as its space.

So if you want the robot to learn the world true,
You need the kind of teacher the world needs in you.

chapters.title: Teaching the World to See
chapters.text:
They walked back towards the train station the long way, through Darling Harbour, because Caleb wanted to see the boats.

The sun was getting low. The water was full of tiny golden dots that danced and shimmered, as if someone had emptied a basket of sequins onto the harbour. Cassie stopped and stared. She remembered the zoom on Mum's phone. She remembered the Million Pictures Wall. She remembered every pixel she had seen all day.

"Look, Caleb," she whispered. "The water is made of pixels today."

Caleb looked. He didn't know what a pixel was, but he knew how to copy his sister. He pointed a chubby finger at a splash of gold and grinned.

"Picks-els!" he cheered. "Picks-els water!"

Cassie felt a warm, buzzy feeling in her chest. It was the feeling of knowing a secret — but a kind secret, the sort you wanted to share. She realised that the whole world was a giant, beautiful puzzle of information, waiting for someone to come along and name the pieces. And the more carefully you named them, the more the world started to make sense.

"Caleb," she said, her voice bright. "Let's play a game. I'll be the teacher. You be the computer."

Caleb loved being a computer. He stood very still and very serious, his light-up sneakers blinking red and blue beneath him.

"See that?" Cassie pointed to a grey bird waddling by.

"Pigeon," Caleb said firmly.

"Correct! And that?" She pointed to a big red vehicle humming along the road.

"Bus."

"And that?" She pointed straight up at the sky.

"Sky!" Caleb shouted, jumping up and down. "Sky-sky-sky!"

"Excellent. And that one?" Cassie pointed to a flag fluttering on a boat.

"Flappy!" Caleb declared.

Cassie laughed. "Close enough. It's a flag. *Flag*."

"Flag," Caleb tried.

"And that?" Cassie pointed at a yellow tower of dough being twisted around behind a bakery window.

Caleb thought hard. "Roti?"

Cassie smiled. "Almost. That's a pretzel. But it does look a bit like roti, doesn't it?" She felt a small thrill, the way Mum had probably felt the first time Cassie called a moon a moon. Teaching, Cassie realised, wasn't just telling somebody the right word. It was watching them try — and noticing what they thought, and why.

Mum was walking behind them, a gentle smile on her face. "You're very good at this, Cassie. You're giving Caleb *labels*."

Cassie paused. "Labels? Like the ones on my school books?"

"Exactly," Mum said. "Think about how the computer learns. A computer doesn't actually know what a 'dog' is. It just sees a pattern of pixels — a pattern of numbers. To teach it, a human has to give it a label. They show the computer ten thousand pictures of dogs and say, 'This pattern is called a Dog.' The computer remembers the pattern, and the label sticks to it. That's how it learns to recognise things. And that's exactly what Dr Fei-Fei Li figured out — that if you want a computer to be smart, you have to give it a *world* full of labelled examples, not just a few easy ones."

Cassie thought about that for a long moment. She watched Caleb confidently shout "BOAT!" at a passing ferry, then "BIG BOAT!" at a slightly larger ferry behind it.

"Mum," she said. "Learning isn't a thing you sit still for. Learning is a thing you *do*."

Mum stopped walking. "Say that again, Cassie."

"Learning is a verb," Cassie said. "It's looking, and wondering, and naming, and getting it wrong sometimes, and trying again. It's not a *thing*. It's a *thing-you-do*."

Mum's eyes were a little shiny. "That's the smartest thing anyone has said today, my love."

"How does it know?" Caleb asked suddenly, pointing at a shimmering fish in the harbour. He was repeating Cassie's question from the morning. The one she had carried around all day like a smooth stone in her pocket.

Cassie beamed.

"It knows because we tell it, Caleb. We show it the world, and we give it the names. And every time we are careful, and fair, and curious about what's missing, the machines learn the world a little better."

Caleb thought about this very seriously. Then he pointed at his own face.

"Caleb," he said proudly.

"Yes," Cassie said. "That's the most important label of all."

That night, the house was quiet. The only sound was the soft rustle of pages as Mum read a bedtime story. When the book closed, Cassie didn't go to sleep right away. She lay in the dark, looking at the glow-in-the-dark stars on her ceiling. They twinkled like the pixels on the harbour water.

"Mum?" she whispered.

"Yes, my love?"

"When I grow up, I want to be a scientist. But I don't just want to make computers smart. I want to teach AIs *nice* things."

Mum paused, her heart swelling. "Nice things? Like what?"

Cassie thought for a long time. The room was full of small ticks and creaks.

"Like how to notice when somebody is sad," she said at last. "And how to see the beauty in a golden puddle. And how to spot every kind of dosa, not just one. And how to make sure that everybody gets a label, not just the people who already had lots of pictures."

Mum leaned over and kissed Cassie's forehead.

"That sounds," she whispered, "like an audacious question to grow into."

Cassie smiled and closed her eyes. She imagined a world where every machine had been taught, by someone like her, to be careful, and curious, and kind.

Downstairs, on the kitchen bench, Mum's phone sat in the moonlight. Inside its memory, a new photograph from the day's trip appeared all by itself. The phone looked at the tiny coloured dots. It saw a pattern — honey-brown skin, wavy black hair, a wide, infectious smile, and dimples.

Because someone, somewhere, had once decided to teach it carefully, the phone quietly attached a label to the image.

*Cassie*.
chapters.poem:
A pigeon, a bus, a flag, a sky,
A dosa, a paratha, a passing fly —
The world is full of things to name,
And learning is a kind of game.

A label here, a label there,
A careful word, a careful care —
The robot only sees as far
As the people teaching it have shown so far.

So look. And wonder. And name what's true.
The world is waiting — kind, and patient, and new —
For the audacious question
That only belongs to you.
